questions.q: What is the common property this lesson identifies across RLHF, Constitutional AI, red-teaming, and refusal training?
options: All four require exactly the same amount of compute to run
All four primarily shape the model's observed behavior, without a built-in guarantee that the change reflects something deeper
All four were invented by the same research lab in the same year
All four eliminate the need for any human involvement whatsoever
questions.explain: Each method, through different mechanisms, shapes what the model outputs. None of them comes with a guarantee that the observed behavior change reflects a deeper internal change.

questions.q: Where does the standard being optimized toward ultimately come from in all four methods?
options: A purely mathematical derivation with no human input
Human judgment, either applied directly (a human rater) or through an intermediate tool (a reward model, or an AI judge grounded in a human-written constitution)
Randomly generated criteria with no connection to human values
The model's own pretraining data, with no external standard at all
questions.explain: Tracing each method's standard back to its source shows it always originates in human judgment, whether that judgment is applied directly or mediated through a trained tool.

questions.q: Why does reliance on human-derived judgment create a scaling problem for alignment methods?
options: Because human judgment is always completely wrong
Because a rater, author, or red-teamer can only reliably evaluate outputs within reach of their own expertise, and that reliability degrades on harder, less verifiable tasks
Because human judgment cannot be used in any machine learning system
Because models always outperform humans on every task simultaneously
questions.explain: The scalability ceiling means judgment-based methods work well where the judge can actually assess quality, and get less reliable as tasks move beyond what the judge can verify.

questions.q: According to this lesson, does the scaling problem described here apply to only one of the four methods covered in this chapter?
options: Yes, it is unique to refusal training
No — it's described as a property of relying on human or human-derived judgment as the alignment target, shared across all four methods
Yes, it only applies to Constitutional AI because it uses a written document
No such problem is described in this lesson
questions.explain: The lesson frames this as a general property of the approach — relying on human-derived judgment — rather than a flaw specific to any single technique.

questions.q: What does this lesson say comes next in the course, and why?
options: Nothing further is needed, since these four methods fully solve alignment
Evaluations first, to measure where models actually stand, followed by scalable oversight techniques aimed at extending training signal beyond what human judges can directly assess
A repeat of RLHF training with more compute
A return to specification gaming from Chapter 1
questions.explain: The lesson sets up the next two chapters as the field's direct response to the judgment-scaling gap: first measuring it through evaluations, then addressing it through scalable oversight.
